title: How Credit Card Companies Make Money (Even If You Pay in Full)

lines: You pay your credit card bill in full, every single month.
You've never paid a cent of interest.
So how is the card company still making money from you?
The answer is hiding in every single tap of your card.
And in a way, even people who pay with cash are paying for it.
Let's follow the money.
When you tap your card, it feels like a deal between just you and the store.
But there are more players involved.
Your bank, which issued your card.
The store's bank, which accepts card payments for the store.
And in the middle, the card network, like Visa or Mastercard, which connects the two banks.
And they all talk to each other in about two seconds.
Here's what happens in those two seconds.
The store's terminal sends your card details to the store's bank.
The store's bank passes the request through the card network.
The network asks your bank: can this person pay?
Your bank checks for fraud and your available credit, and says yes or no.
The answer travels all the way back, and the terminal beeps.
The actual money moves later, usually within a day or two, when the payments are settled.
Now, let's say you buy something for one hundred dollars.
The store doesn't actually receive one hundred dollars.
A slice is taken out before the money arrives.
It's called the swipe fee.
For Visa and Mastercard credit cards in the United States, merchant groups put the average swipe fee at around two point three percent in 2025.
So on a one hundred dollar sale, the store keeps roughly ninety-seven dollars and change.
Most of that slice is the interchange fee, and it goes to your bank, the one that issued your card.
The store's bank adds a small markup for handling the payment.
And the card network charges the banks its own, much smaller, fees for running the system.
Here's what surprises a lot of people.
Visa and Mastercard don't keep the interchange fee.
They earn their money from network and processing fees instead.
Two percent sounds tiny.
But Americans put trillions of dollars on their cards every year.
Merchant groups estimate that Visa and Mastercard credit card swipe fees alone came to well over one hundred billion dollars in 2025.
And your bank earns its share of that even if you never pay a single cent of interest.
So why would any store agree to give up two percent of every sale?
Because people spend more easily with cards, and many barely carry cash anymore.
A store that refuses cards can lose customers.
So most stores simply accept the fee as a cost of doing business.
This is also where your rewards come from.
Cash back, points and airline miles are largely paid for by these swipe fees.
Premium rewards cards usually carry higher swipe fees for the store.
So your bank collects a bigger slice, and hands part of it back to you as points.
You're not getting free money. You're getting a share of the fee the store paid.
But the store has to cover that fee somehow.
Usually, it builds the cost into its prices, for everyone.
A study by the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston found that this means people who pay with cash end up helping to fund the rewards of people who pay with cards.
And because rewards cards are used more by higher income households, the money tends to flow from lower income shoppers to higher income ones.
Now, the swipe fee is just one stream of money.
The biggest one comes from people who don't pay in full.
Americans owed about one point two eight trillion dollars on their credit cards at the end of 2025, according to the New York Fed.
And on accounts that were charged interest, the average rate in 2025 was around twenty-two percent a year, according to the Federal Reserve.
The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau found that cardholders paid about one hundred sixty billion dollars in interest in 2024.
Plus more than thirty billion dollars in fees.
Those fees come in many forms.
Annual fees on premium cards.
Late payment fees.
Cash advance fees.
And foreign transaction fees when you pay abroad.
So how does a credit card company make money, even from you?
One: the swipe fee on every purchase, paid by the store.
Two: interest from people who carry a balance.
Three: fees.
If you pay in full every month, you only feed the first stream.
And you even get part of it back as rewards.
It's the people carrying a balance who pay for the biggest part of the business.
So next time you tap your card, remember: about two seconds, five players, and a slice for almost everyone.
